On the morning arranged for Admiral and Mrs Croft to visit Kellynch Hall, Anne felt it was quite natural to take her usual, almost daily walk to Lady Russell’s and stay away until the visit was over. Afterwards, she felt it was equally natural to regret missing her chance to meet them.

The meeting pleased everyone and settled the whole matter immediately. Both ladies had already been inclined to agree, and each therefore noticed only the other’s good manners. As for the gentlemen, the Admiral showed such warm good humour and such an open, generous trust that Sir Walter could hardly fail to respond. Mr Shepherd had also encouraged Sir Walter’s finest and most elegant behaviour by assuring him that the Admiral already knew of him by reputation as a perfect example of good breeding.

The house, grounds, and furniture met with approval; so did the Crofts. The terms, the date, everything and everyone were satisfactory. Mr Shepherd’s clerks began preparing the agreement without a single earlier disagreement to be resolved in any part of that document beginning, “This agreement states.”

Sir Walter declared without hesitation that the Admiral was the best-looking sailor he had ever met. He even said that, if his own servant could have arranged the Admiral’s hair, he would not have been ashamed to be seen with him anywhere. The Admiral returned this kindness in his own way. As they drove back through the park, he remarked to his wife, “I thought we should soon reach an agreement, my dear, despite what they told us at Taunton. The Baronet will never do anything brilliant, but there seems to be no harm in him.”—compliments on both sides which might have been considered roughly equal.

The Crofts were to take possession at Michaelmas. Since Sir Walter intended to move to Bath during the month before that, there was no time to waste in making all the other arrangements that depended on the move.

Lady Russell was certain that Anne would not be allowed to help, or have any influence, in choosing the house they were to rent. She was therefore very reluctant to see her hurried away so soon. She hoped to arrange for Anne to stay behind until she could take her to Bath herself after Christmas. But Lady Russell had commitments of her own that would take her away from Kellynch for several weeks, so she could not offer the full invitation she wanted to give. Anne dreaded the heat they might still have in September among the dazzling white buildings of Bath. She also grieved at giving up the country’s autumn months, with all their sweet and sorrowful influence on her feelings. Even so, when she considered everything, she did not think she wished to stay.

“So I own a few knights now,” said I, as we rode away. “Who could have imagined I should live to put property of that description on my books. I shan’t know what to do with them, short of holding a raffle. How many have I got, Sandy?”

“Seven, an it please you, sir, with their squires.”

“A handsome catch. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes, where do they make their homes?”

“Ah, I took not thy meaning. That shall I tell thee eftsoons.” Then, thoughtfully and in a low voice, she rolled the words delicately upon her tongue: “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out; ay, even so; where do they hang out. Truly the saying hath a sweet and pleasant grace, and is fashioned prettily withal. I shall rehearse it now and again in mine idle hours, that perchance I may learn it. Where do they hang out. Aye, so! Already it runneth lightly off my tongue, and inasmuch as—”

“Don’t lose sight of the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes, the knights, you understand. You meant to tell me about them. Some time ago, if you remember. Speaking figuratively, play’s been called.”

“Play—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Step up to bat. That is, begin on your statistics, and don’t use up so much kindling lighting your fire. Tell me about those knights.”

“Gladly will I, and swiftly shall begin. So those two went away and rode into a mighty forest. And—”

“Great Scott!”

You see, I perceived my blunder immediately. I had put her machinery in motion; the fault was mine; she would take thirty days to reach those facts. Besides, she commonly started without an introduction and ended without arriving anywhere. If you broke in, she either proceeded without paying attention, or replied in a word or two, went back, and repeated the entire sentence. Interrupting, then, merely made matters worse; nevertheless I was obliged to interrupt, and quite often at that, to preserve my life. A man would perish if he let that monotony trickle over him steadily the whole day.

“Great Scott!” I cried in my misery. She returned straight to the beginning:

“So those two went away and rode into a mighty forest. And—”

“Which two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. And thus they reached an abbey of monks, where they were lodged well. In the morning they heard their masses in the abbey, then rode onward until they entered a great forest; there Sir Gawaine espied, in a valley beside a turret, twelve beautiful damsels and two knights in armour upon great horses, and the damsels walked back and forth beside a tree.

Presently they went past deserted brickfields. Here the fog thinned, and he could distinguish the curious bottle-shaped kilns, with their orange tongues of flame spreading like fans. A dog barked at their passing, and somewhere far off in the blackness a straying sea-gull shrieked. The horse tripped in a rut, then shied to one side and began to gallop.

After a while they turned off the clay road and rattled once more along roughly paved streets. The greater part of the windows were unlit, though here and there grotesque shadows stood out upon a blind illuminated by a lamp. He observed them with curiosity. They stirred like enormous marionettes, gesticulating like living creatures. He loathed them. A heavy anger filled his heart. When they rounded a corner, a woman shouted something after them from an open doorway, and two men pursued the hansom for a hundred yards or so. The driver struck at them with his whip.

They say that passion drives thought round in circles. Certainly, with dreadful repetition, Dorian Gray’s bitten lips formed and formed again those delicate phrases concerning soul and sense, until he discovered in them, as it were, the complete utterance of his mood. Thus he sanctioned with his intellect passions which, even without that sanction, would have governed his temper. The single thought stole from cell to cell within his brain; and the fierce longing to live, most fearful of all human appetites, stirred every quivering nerve and fibre into power. Ugliness, which he had formerly detested for making things real, was precious to him now for precisely that cause. Ugliness alone was real. The vulgar quarrel, the repulsive den, the rough violence of chaotic living, the sheer baseness of outcast and thief, impressed him with an actuality more intensely vivid than all art’s lovely forms and all song’s visionary shadows. These were the things he required if he was to forget. Three days more, and he would be free.

Without warning the driver pulled up sharply at the head of a dark lane. Above the houses’ low roofs and uneven chimney-stacks stood the black masts of ships. White coils of mist hung about the yards like spectral sails.

“Round here somewheres, sir, ain’t it?” he inquired hoarsely through the trap.

Dorian gave a start and looked about him. “This will do,” he replied. He climbed out quickly, paid the driver the additional fare he had promised, and hurried towards the quay. At intervals a lantern shone from the stern of a great merchant ship. Its reflection trembled and broke into fragments in the puddles. A steamer taking on coal before sailing cast a crimson glow. The slippery pavement had the appearance of a rain-soaked mackintosh.
